title: We Replaced Our Sales Team With AI – Here’s What Happened | Santos Sharan & Amit Vasudev
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson is explicitly absent: the host says he is spending time with his family at 00:00:44–00:00:50. The main host is addressed as Pete; his surname is not established. The main guests are Santos Sharan and Amit Vasudev, with names supplied by metadata and introduction despite caption variations. Audience participants Bernie, founder of Latitude 39, and Gabriel, founder of an unnamed aesthetic-clinic software company, also speak. Some audience advice is read aloud by Pete. Speaker assignments are inferred from conversational context because captions lack diarization. The closing passage at 00:57:14–00:57:34 appears to transition into a teaser with uncertain speakers. No statement in this source is securely attributable to Adam speaking firsthand.
summary: This episode introduces Santos and Amit’s planned AI platform for business research and purchasing, captioned inconsistently as Zer, zir, and zero. They discuss founder fit, temporary stealth, defensibility, platform development through micro apps, and how cheaper software creation could change venture financing. Their central thesis is that increasingly crowded software markets require better buyer research and control, including agents that attend vendor calls and recommend context-specific solutions. The product is presented as forthcoming, without demonstrated revenue, replacement of a sales team, or measured operating results. An audience segment explores distribution for aesthetic-clinic software. Adam-related evidence is limited to host statements about RB2B and Adam’s activities.

key_learnings.claim: Bernie positions incentive-compensation software around three buyer outcomes: less administrative work, fewer calculation errors, and better sales behavior through visibility into compensation.
key_learnings.speaker: Bernie
key_learnings.caveat: Latitude 39’s sales pitch; claimed outcomes are not independently demonstrated or quantified.

key_learnings.claim: Santos views shared experience, frustration with the same problem, and compatible life stages as important co-founder selection criteria alongside relevant skills.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Explains his own founding-team decision, not Adam’s hiring philosophy.

key_learnings.claim: Pete argues that working compatibility can justify choosing a somewhat less talented colleague over a difficult but highly talented one.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete
key_learnings.caveat: Host opinion; no specific hiring outcome is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Santos still favors transparency and building in public. His temporary stealth period reflected unresolved product direction, an incomplete founding team, and unfinished incorporation and website logistics.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: This is a boundary condition for disclosure, not an endorsement of secrecy as a competitive moat.

key_learnings.claim: Pete sees value in delaying a public launch while the idea remains exploratory and repeated pivots appear likely.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete
key_learnings.caveat: Host interpretation of the guests’ circumstances, not a universal requirement to finish a product before sharing it.

key_learnings.claim: Santos believes easier copying shifts defensibility toward distribution, community, network effects, and business-model innovation, while increasing the appeal of platforms over isolated tools.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Strategic thesis about the AI era; not proof that technology moats have disappeared.

key_learnings.claim: The founders plan to build a platform incrementally through monthly micro apps whose initially separate use cases eventually connect into one experience.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Planned methodology. No completed platform or sustained shipping cadence is demonstrated.

key_learnings.claim: Amit treats speed of execution and repeated value delivery across multiple use cases as potential advantages. At Clearbit, customers could arrive for one problem and adopt another solution.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Retrospective guest experience and current strategy; no cross-sell or retention figures are provided.

key_learnings.claim: Amit preserves important exceptions to the copying thesis: hard technology, data network effects, and systems of record can still offer technological or structural defensibility.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: He says defensibility is harder for thin SaaS, rather than impossible for all software.

key_learnings.claim: Amit recommends examining both practical and emotional reasons to adopt and stay: accumulated memory or state, continued value, identity or status, and an authentic connection to the product.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Conceptual framework; the episode does not show these mechanisms working in the new venture.

key_learnings.claim: Amit describes an ecosystem advantage when others build on a platform and depend on it for distribution, making its value broader than its own feature set.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Proposed source of defensibility, not an achieved network effect.

key_learnings.claim: Amit wants trust and brand to come from solving problems consistently. He warns that excessive podcast promotion can displace product work and cannot substitute for product-market fit.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: A limit on promotional activity, not a rejection of brand marketing.

key_learnings.claim: Santos expects more competing alternatives and fewer unicorns as software becomes easier to build, while still seeing opportunities for venture investment and faster entrepreneurial progress.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Forecast, not an observed count of unicorns or a recommendation that every founder bootstrap.

key_learnings.claim: Amit thinks the predictable progression from initial SaaS scale to a large IPO has weakened as markets fragment, but exceptional products can still grow rapidly and become very valuable.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Prediction supported by qualitative examples; the captioned company name 'Ryder' is uncertain.

key_learnings.claim: Amit distinguishes improved capital efficiency from eliminating capital needs: strong growth can attract financing, and large successful companies may still use substantial cash effectively.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Conversational attribution is inferred; no financing plan for the new venture is disclosed.

key_learnings.claim: Gabriel is entering a crowded clinic-CRM market through a narrow image-management product that addresses an immediate workflow before attempting the broader CRM vision.
key_learnings.speaker: Gabriel
key_learnings.caveat: Early-stage strategy with only a first paying user reported; expansion into the full system is an ambition.

key_learnings.claim: Gabriel identifies a distribution mismatch: LinkedIn makes prospects easy to find, but clinic owners present there tend to run larger practices with stronger existing processes than his intended customers.
key_learnings.speaker: Gabriel
key_learnings.caveat: Founder observation without a measured channel comparison.

key_learnings.claim: Pete reports that RB2B customers selling to doctors and dentists struggled to connect through business-profile data, and suggests testing direct clinic calls because these professionals still work on site.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete
key_learnings.caveat: Anecdotal customer feedback. Gabriel had not tested calling and anticipated receptionist barriers.

key_learnings.claim: Santos recommends exploring Facebook, Instagram, and consumer-oriented data sources for clinic outreach instead of assuming conventional B2B lists and LinkedIn are the right channels.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Untested advice for Gabriel’s case. A possible Retention contact is suggested, without a verified solution.

key_learnings.claim: Audience advice relayed by Pete suggests building relationships with receptionists and marketing managers as internal champions, and using referrals to reach healthcare customers.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete, relaying audience comments
key_learnings.caveat: Originates partly with unnamed commenters and Michael Hopkins; no result is reported.

key_learnings.claim: Santos says buyer and seller interviews revealed rising search costs, distrust of vendor-sponsored content, and poor purchasing decisions that later create seller churn problems.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Founders’ synthesis of their own research; sampling, interview questions, and underlying evidence are unavailable.

key_learnings.claim: Santos argues that another seller-outreach automation will lose effectiveness as it spreads, and instead proposes less interruption and more buyer-led, problem-focused research.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Strategic reassessment from someone who built seller tools; the forecast about rapid loss of effectiveness is untested here.

key_learnings.claim: Amit uses Clearbit to illustrate vendor bias: a buyer seeking better website conversion would receive a Clearbit-centered answer from its salesperson, even if another approach better fit the underlying problem.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Guest retrospective and illustrative account, not a quantified audit of sales recommendations.

key_learnings.claim: Amit proposes a buyer-centered research service that uses changing, unstructured information to recommend suitable solutions, rather than letting vendor SEO, outreach, or social visibility determine consideration.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Product vision. Criticisms of review sites and research providers are guest opinions, not independently verified findings.

key_learnings.claim: The proposed platform would learn company context and use agents for meetings, research, peer and vendor introductions, playbooks, and purchasing workflows. Its first planned app lets an agent take vendor discovery calls for a buyer.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Forthcoming capabilities, not a demonstrated deployment. The company name and URL are unclear in captions.

key_learnings.claim: Amit wants agents to progress beyond returning information into completing research actions, such as obtaining prices, attending demos, and potentially testing trials. He says interviewed vendors liked the possibility of pitching a buyer’s agent when the buyer was otherwise inaccessible.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Mix of product ambition and qualitative interview feedback; no completed trial automation or conversion result is shown.

key_learnings.claim: Santos says the broader platform would also serve sellers by delivering buyers who have completed much of their evaluation through automation.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan

key_learnings.claim: Santos describes bot-to-bot calls as structured information exchanges: each bot receives content or a short briefing and enters with an agenda resembling a form to complete.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: This does not establish resistance to deception. His dismissal of risk and the ensuing efficiency prediction lack supporting tests.

key_learnings.claim: Amit makes buyer opt-in a stated design principle: buyers should control whom they engage with and how, rather than having their activity automatically sold to vendors.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Declared product intention; implementation, monetization, and enforcement are not described.

key_learnings.claim: Amit says a useful recommendation engine should consider vendors, combinations of tools, consultants, agents, and building internally. The answer should depend on the company’s context and preferences and improve as that context accumulates.
key_learnings.speaker: Amit Vasudev
key_learnings.caveat: Future functionality. He emphasizes improvement within one company, not only benefits from adding more companies.

key_learnings.claim: Santos identifies proprietary company context from meetings and other data as the intended distinction from generic AI research, including the ability to consolidate unstructured requirements from a buying committee.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan
key_learnings.caveat: Claimed differentiation and intended functionality; no comparative evaluation or working committee workflow is demonstrated.

key_learnings.claim: The closing poll explores willingness to delegate internal meetings, external meetings, webinars, research, and introductions to agents, treating the extent of user trust as a product-discovery question.
key_learnings.speaker: Santos Sharan

tensions_and_corrections: The title claims a sales team was replaced with AI and implies results. The transcript instead presents a forthcoming buyer-agent product, with no identified sales-team replacement, eliminated roles, revenue impact, or measured experiment.
Adam is explicitly absent. Guest strategies, Clearbit experiences, and the new venture’s plans must not become Adam’s beliefs or achievements. RB2B’s $5 million ARR milestone is a host report.

Pete frames stealth against the risk of copying after RB2B’s public launch. Santos explains his own stealth as temporary exploration and logistics while retaining a preference for transparency; the source does not establish a change of mind toward secrecy.
The stealth duration varies between approximately three months and two and a half months. Neither estimate should be silently converted into an exact chronology.
Santos’s broad claim that AI software will be copied is narrowed by Amit’s acknowledgment of hard-tech, data-network, and system-of-record moats.

The founders expect fragmentation to weaken the old VC scaling playbook, while also recognizing that exceptional companies can attract capital and reach very large valuations. This is not a categorical anti-VC position.

Brand and community are presented as advantages, but Amit says promotion cannot shortcut product-market fit. Pete’s claim that the team overdid podcasts is his retrospective assessment, not Adam’s confession.
The buyer-centered platform also intends to serve sellers. Amit promises buyer opt-in, but the episode does not explain the monetization model or how recommendation neutrality will be preserved.

When Pete asks about bots deceiving each other, Santos largely dismisses the risk and explains structured agendas. No adversarial testing, factual verification, or evidence supporting the dismissal is supplied.
Amit predicts more efficient bot discovery calls; Santos’s 80–90% evaluation-completion figure is a vision. Neither constitutes measured performance.
The platform is described with confident capability language alongside a future first-app launch and beta waitlist. Treat availability and effectiveness as unproven at publication.
Pete loosely describes ARR as money being brought in at 00:24:23–00:24:33. Keep ARR separate from recognized revenue, profit, and cash collections.
Gabriel’s statement that image approval means no privacy risk is broader than the evidence supports. The transcript establishes only his stated consent requirement.

Names and URLs are repeatedly garbled: the new company appears as Zer, zir, zero, and truncated 'z.'; other examples include 'exactly,' 'Ryder,' and 'gardener.' Do not silently reconstruct definitive identities or URLs from these captions.
At 00:53:18–00:53:31 Pete associates November 2022 with the first LLM reaching the market. This imprecise historical aside should not be entered as verified AI history.
The final 20 seconds appear to be a teaser or edited transition. Speaker attribution and the precise startup approach being discussed remain uncertain.
